rv.q: From its pitch-perfect prologue to its enigmatic epilogue, this maximalist blockbuster mesmerizes at every turn.
Now, with the final show of the 2025-26 crop, he’s delivered the best.
The Lost Boys, the Michael Arden-directed stage adaptation of the 1987 movie about teenage bloodsuckers, opens tonight at the Palace Theatre, and it’s killer fun.
"The Lost Boys" never stops moving, managing to be at once kinetic and poetic, earnestly emotional and rock-and-roll bombastic.
This stunner of a show, based on the Joel Schumacher film, is a solid theatrical transformation, rich in imagination, humor and heart — and with spectacular special effects.

Arden and scenic designer Dane Laffrey, whose past collaborations include Maybe Happy Ending and A Christmas Carol, have again created a world we’ve never seen onstage before: surprising, thrilling, sometimes genuinely unsettling.
And this bawdy crowd-pleaser at least has the courage of its crackpot convictions.
The Lost Boys contains the finest spectacle I have seen this season outside of the Met Opera.
Ultimately, when this kind of scale manages to bring with it both genuine humor and beauty, I'm pulled toward enjoyment.

The Palace is a big venue of course and, for many hinterland punters, “The Lost Boys” will deliver an epic Broadway blast, an amped-up escape from their prosaic realities and that will do it for a vampire musical.
Although the score, by the rock band the Rescues, is a cut above most Broadway pop, the musical is nevertheless overscaled, over-earnest and overlong.
The high production value of The Lost Boys may leave hipper audiences yearning for a firmer commitment to style over substance – rather than its ultimate choice of sap over style.
It’s the best new musical on Broadway.
The Lost Boys is a big and bold production marrying technical enchantment with a talented cast of vocal heavyweights.
The Lost Boys, with its addictive sense of whimsical wonder, is soaring all on its own.
“The Lost Boys” is, in other words, a theatrical crowd-pleaser.
The Lost Boys is quite likely to make the short list.
Those elements, along with Markus Maurette’s special effects, could be considered worth the price of admission.

Can any show break the curse of failed vampire-driven musicals? Following belatedly in the footsteps of the ill-crafted “Lestat,” “Dance of the Vampires” and “Dracula” is “The Lost Boys,” now at the Palace Theatre. And there may not be enough garlic or wooden stakes in America to ward off this adapt...
Although Michael is courting David’s co-lead singer, the vivacious Star (Maria Wirries), his corrosive bond with the predatory David renders the rest of the musical’s relationships forgettable.
But there's a catch: Despite all the good work onstage -- including a couple of extremely strong performances -- The Lost Boys is yet another musical that struggles to sing.
The cumulative effect is undeniably exciting. Mainstream audiences will likely feel they are seeing an event.
If you’re going for sheer Broadway spectacle, there’s a lot to enjoy in The Lost Boys.

Too much of the score, though, feels forgettable, one pop ballad bleeding into another and too redolent of the sort of bombastic power ballads that hair bands routinely pumped out in the nineties (much of it also has the feeling of Christian rock).
And while none are fatal, there are enough to keep The Lost Boys from achieving that one thing vampires and Broadway musicals desire more than anything else – eternal life.
“The Lost Boys” doesn’t know what it wants to be: a shocker, a tear-jerker or a parody.
If such gimmicks and a lot of noise, plus a little preaching, add up to a satisfying night at the theater for you, “The Lost Boys” could be just your ticket.
If anything, “The Lost Boys” is worse than all of them.
But for all the expense and effort, The Lost Boys is, to this observer, a lost cause.
The Lost Boys: A New Musical is an astounding production.
It’s a thrill ride from start to finish.
The Lost Boys is a wildly entertaining night at the theater: funny, frightening, heartfelt, and irresistibly cool.
The Lost Boys delivers a gleefully propulsive blockbuster that breaks Broadway’s vampire musical curse and gives a desperate season exactly what it needs.

The Lost Boys may be the most spectacular surprise of the Broadway season — a visually captivating show that actually improves on its source material with more fleshed-out characters, a more coherent plot, and a hook-filled rock score that deepens our connection to both the players and their plight.
The Lost Boys is Broadway’s splashiest opening in years, with nostalgia-feeding IP, gravity-defying F/X, and a hard-working cast of pros and fresh faces.
Some creatures are better left in the dark.
This clever and creative stage adaptation is wildly impressive from the second the curtain goes up until the moment the company takes its final bow.
The Lost Boys had its official opening night earlier this week and, as you can probably tell, we really loved it.
The Lost Boys will lure you in and keep you thoroughly entertained.
